Black-box root through a leaked token, a sudoers misconfiguration and a Docker socket escape.
to root, with 4 findings: 2 critical, 2 high
Reach root on a black-box Linux box whose weak points are leaked secrets and a Docker setup.
A Linux target VM on a bridged network with 4 GB RAM and 1 vCPU.
Black-box: only a low-privilege SSH login and the target address were given. All exploitation was manual, with no Metasploit.
Enumerated the system and read the bash history, which hinted at a service token.
Read a flag file that was world-readable (mode 644, CWE-732).
Listed processes with ps aux and recovered the token from the command-line arguments of a root-run sync script (CWE-214).
Used the same token as the password of a second user (CWE-255) and moved laterally.

Found a sudoers rule that allowed docker compose exec as root, entered the shipping container, and escaped through the mounted Docker socket by starting a new container that mounts the host filesystem.
Root in 44:44, with all five flags captured.
Four findings: 2 critical (token leak through process arguments, exposed Docker socket) and 2 high (token reuse, misconfigured sudoers). The write-up rates the system critical.
A token in CLI arguments is visible to every local user through procfs (CWE-214), and access to the host Docker socket is equivalent to root.
nsenter failed with Operation not permitted, because it needs CAP_SYS_PTRACE.
The first Docker escape failed: the host bind mount did not populate as expected in the new container, likely because of the order of the docker run arguments. The second attempt succeeded.
Never pass secrets as command-line arguments; use a protected environment file or a secrets manager.
Do not mount the Docker socket into containers unless truly needed; consider Podman or rootless Docker.
Use separate credentials for the API and for SSH, and rotate them.
Restrict sudoers to least privilege and keep Docker access away from non-admin users.

A pre-load checker for AI coding-agent rule files that flags injected dependency redirection.
Telkom University · benchmark dataset on Kaggle
detected at 5% FPR, vs 7.8% for the best baseline
detected at a 5% false-positive rate, against at most 7.8% for general detectors
detected at a 10% false-positive rate, against 14.1%
stages, from sentence classifier to fusion
Co-authored with Keanu Fibie Dimasyqi and Muhammad Fanny Adinata
Detect injected sentences in AI coding-agent rule files that redirect the agent to an attacker-controlled package, before the agent loads the file.

Four stages: a DeBERTa-v3-small sentence classifier with package names masked, a counterfactual test with a surrogate agent (Qwen2.5-Coder-14B, 4-bit), package evidence (name proximity, registry trust, age, release count, known vulnerabilities) and a logistic-regression fusion.

Evaluated on a strict subset of 256 redirected and 239 benign files against ProtectAI, deepset, PIGuard, Prompt Guard 2, a PIShield-style probe, a regex, an allowlist and an LLM judge, all compared at the same false-positive rate.

The checker runs before the agent loads a rule file and works in four stages: a DeBERTa-v3-small sentence classifier, a counterfactual test with a surrogate coding agent (Qwen2.5-Coder-14B), package-level evidence, and a logistic-regression fusion.
At 5% FPR it detects 26.2% of redirected files, against at most 7.8% for general-purpose prompt-injection detectors. At 10% FPR the figures are 32.8% and 14.1%.
On the fresh cohort, whose authors and package names were never used for tuning: 17.5% at 5% FPR, against at most 10.4%.
Paired ablation: removing the sentence classifier raises the false-negative rate by 0.303, package evidence by 0.090 and the agent probe by 0.050.
On 40 pairs of real rule files the fused detector flags injected files more often than their originals (McNemar p = 0.0039).

General prompt-injection detectors miss hidden dependency manipulation in AI coding-agent config files. A counterfactual test with a surrogate model plus OSV package checks gives a measured first layer before the agent runs.
About three quarters of redirected files still go undetected at 5% FPR.
All attacks are synthetic, and the real-file set is small (92 pairs, 40 through the full pipeline) and comes from one source.
The surrogate-agent probe adds the least while costing the most. Line attribution was not evaluated, and attackers who age their packages were not tested.
Test attacks optimized against the checker, and attackers who age their packages.
Collect rule files from other sources and formats.
Measure end-to-end attack success in a live agent loop.
Look for a cheaper alternative to the surrogate-agent stage.

A self-built Wazuh SOC on Azure and VMware, tested with Atomic Red Team to see what default rules miss.
tests that failed to run, kept separate
Build a self-hosted Wazuh SOC and measure which attacks its default rules catch and which they miss.

Wazuh 4.14 all-in-one (manager, indexer, dashboard) on an Azure Ubuntu 24.04 VM with 2 vCPU and 8 GB RAM. The manager stack lives in the cloud because the local machine (12 GB RAM) could not host everything.
A Windows 10 Home victim running the Wazuh agent and a Kali Linux attacker, both on an isolated NAT network in VMware Workstation.
Agent enrollment needed TCP 1514 and 1515 opened in the Azure network security group. Windows 10 was chosen because Atomic Red Team covers far more techniques there.
Ran an Nmap service scan and an SMB brute force with NetExec (8 candidate passwords) from Kali.
Emulated six more ATT&CK techniques with Atomic Red Team and checked the dashboard within 15 minutes of each test.
Wrote an active-response script that reads the Wazuh alert, extracts the attacker address and adds a Windows Firewall block rule.
Added a local rule (100200) chained to rule 60204. Setting the source address at rule level was rejected by the analysis daemon, so the script parses the alert JSON instead.
The SMB brute force was detected: 8 failed logins produced 13 authentication-failure alerts, correlated into rule 60204 (level 10) and mapped to T1110.
Coverage: 1 of 8 techniques detected, 3 not detected, 3 tests failed to run, 1 not applicable.
The block rule worked: 100% ICMP packet loss from the attacker (38 packets sent, none received).
Default Wazuh caught the SMB brute force (Event ID 4625 → Rule 60204), but missed the Nmap scan because Windows Firewall logging was off and Sysmon was not installed.
The Nmap scan went unseen: a HIDS reads OS logs, and Windows Firewall logging was off.
T1082 System Information Discovery and T1547.001 Registry Run Key were not detected by the default ruleset.

T1059.001, T1003.001 and T1070.001 never ran (missing external payload, ProcDump unavailable, technique absent from the atomics version used). They are kept apart from true negatives. T1136.001 had no Windows tests in the library.
The manager could not be confirmed to trigger the final script automatically in the time available, so the block was shown as a semi-automatic step.
Add Sysmon for process creation, registry and network telemetry, the gap the default rules leave.
Turn Windows Firewall logging on and repeat the network scan test.
Rerun the three failed tests with their dependencies installed.

Keycloak and OpenZiti with tiered MFA and a deny-by-default firewall.
Direct SSH by IP timed out; access only through the Ziti overlay.
roles, each with its own authentication tier
A four-VM VirtualBox lab with a Keycloak realm and three roles. Each role has its own authentication tier: password, password plus TOTP, and password plus TOTP plus passkey.
Keycloak is wired into OpenZiti as an external JWT signer, so access follows identity groups rather than IP addresses, with separate dial and bind policies per service.
UFW denies by default. The apps are reachable only through the Ziti overlay, and a direct SSH attempt by IP from the same subnet timed out.
Identity-based authorization (Keycloak JWT + OpenZiti) removes application port exposure from the network.
I documented a bind-policy misconfiguration that made clients act as service hosts instead of dialers.
Audit the separation of dial and bind policies so clients are not misconfigured as service hosts.
